summary:
Same-sex relations are criminalised in Eswatini for men and women throughout the country, as of 12 March 2026. No legal gender recognition is available, so a trans visitor's passport and other identity documents are read exactly as issued, with no administrative route to align them with lived gender.

Eswatini recognises no same-sex relationships. A trans visitor travelling in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship falls under the criminal law. In June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said that people of the same sex could not even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not ready to consider the question; in 2014 press secretary Percy Simelane said the government was monitoring the situation with a view to taking a legal position.

No registered national advocacy body exists to turn to for help. The registrar of companies refused in June 2019 to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities on grounds of morality, and refused a further LGBTI group in July 2019. In April 2022 the High Court upheld the refusal to register ESGM while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. Outright International reports that LGBTI organisations cannot register as of 12 March 2026.

There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Rock of Hope states that with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa.

Access to care carries a documented risk of refusal. A 2019 survey found 59% of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities, and 30% denied healthcare services. Policy runs the other way: section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion, and in February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, with Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane saying the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples.

Targeted violence is documented with dates. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. The most recent documented case in this record is from 2015; no later instance is documented.

Official hostility is on the record. The US State Department's 2021 report noted that some traditional, religious and government officials criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In 2012 former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law, saying so few gays lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort; in May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of one's sex or sexual orientation, define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity, and name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence. These policy instruments sit beneath a criminal law that has not changed.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House's Freedom in the World 2024 rates Eswatini Not Free with an overall score of 17/100, comprising Political Rights 1/40 and Civil Liberties 16/60, describing an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space. The BTI 2024 country report places the refusal to register LGBTQ+ groups within a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment, in an environment where 'Mswati must fall' had become a common protest slogan. Civic space is closed for political organising generally, not only for LGBTI bodies.

Public visibility has nonetheless been documented. The first Eswatini Pride was held in July 2018 and declared a great success, and in June 2021 LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident. In December 2018 a church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened, recorded alongside no let-up on discrimination in the kingdom. These events took place while same-sex conduct remained illegal and do not alter the legal position.

The 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation.
localsOnly:
Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced. There is no legal recognition of same-sex relationships, so a resident couple has no route to registration, inheritance or next-of-kin standing through relationship status.

Residents have no statutory discrimination remedy in education, health, housing or employment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Limited protections exist in policy: the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation, and the National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles.

Historical survey data on resident mental health: a 2013 survey found 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances to feel normal. The figure covers that survey year only and is not a current prevalence measure.

Organisational registration remains closed to LGBTI groups, which removes the ordinary channel through which residents would form an association, hold meetings or recruit. Rock of Hope's assessment is that LGBTQ people stay in the closet or leave for a neighbouring jurisdiction rather than live openly.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific killing or violence rate for Eswatini is sourced here, and no general homicide rate is available for comparison, so no trans violence magnitude can be stated. The two documented killings in this record are individual incidents from 2015 and earlier, not a rate.

The healthcare discrimination figures (59% and 30%) come from a 2019 survey of LGBTQ people broadly, not trans people specifically, and the window closed in 2019; no later measurement of healthcare treatment is sourced. The 2013 suicide and substance figures likewise cover lesbian and transgender respondents in that survey year only.

Whether any administrative practice exists for amending gender markers on foreign passports at the border, or how Eswatini border officials treat documents that do not match presentation, is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved. No entry, visa or screening rule specific to trans travellers is documented here.

The April 2022 High Court judgment accepted constitutional protections for association, privacy and expression while upholding the registration refusal; whether that reasoning has been applied to any later registration application is not sourced and remains unresolved.
